clue.text: Magic performer, big hitter

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who performs brilliantly, a terrific person
second meaning: one who hits hard, as in tennis

explanation.surface: A conjuror who also happens to be a powerful striker of the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magic' is British slang for excellent, so a 'magic performer' is an outstanding one; that is not a conjuror at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Smasher is informal British praise for a wonderful person, and literally names whoever smashes the ball hard.

clue.text: Neat and evergreen

definitions.meaning: first meaning: smart and tidy in appearance

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a description of a tidy hedge, but these are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means smartly turned out, and the noun names a coniferous tree that keeps its needles all year.

clue.text: Grand time?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a month of the year

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand time' sounds like a lovely occasion; split it into an adjective and a period of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means majestic or venerable, and as a proper noun it is the eighth month, a span of time.

clue.text: Classic competitor, say, maverick was hero on Mondays, primarily

indicators.note: a maverick refuses to stay in line, so the letters break their order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: first letter of Mondays

explanation.surface: A tribute: the nonconformist setter was a Monday hero, a classic competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Classics are the great flat races in British horse racing, and a rider in one fits 'Classic competitor, say'. Rufus set the Guardian's Monday cryptic.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman riding in a Classic horse race is one example of a female rider, hence the 'say'.

clue.text: Another test penned by 5 across I treasured

indicators.note: something penned by others is enclosed within their words

parts.note: 5 across is SQUIRES, so the run reads SQUIRES I TREASURED and the letters lie across the join

explanation.surface: A second exam written by a much-loved setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Replace '5 across' with its answer, then the letters straddle the end of that surname and the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is a second sitting of an exam that was failed, so it is another test.

clue.text: Gentlemen, last seen of genius on paper

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece sitting on another simply goes before it
the last thing seen of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: final letter of genius
a quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: A tribute: the last glimpse of a genius is what he left behind on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is also the surname of the late setter Roger Squires, who compiled as Rufus.
explanation.definitionFit: Squires were country landowners, the traditional English gentry, so the plural stands for gentlemen.

clue.text: Specimens after action, those taken away

indicators.note: after says the first-named piece follows the second in the answer

parts.note: a legal action is a lawsuit
cases are instances or examples

explanation.surface: Scientific samples being removed after some procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken away' sounds like removal, but it means taken on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Luggage is what travellers take away with them on a trip, so these are things taken away.

clue.text: Able to depart rocky Shetland isle

indicators.note: the named word departs, leaving the rest of the longer word behind

parts.note: rocky means shaky
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: Someone can leave a rocky island in Shetland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able' looks like 'can', but it is the very letters to take out. Shetland is the island group north of mainland Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Unst is the most northerly inhabited island of the Shetland archipelago.

clue.text: Extracts from Haley novel published

parts.note: Alex Haley's novel about his family's history
a book that is published is out

explanation.surface: Quotations taken from an Alex Haley novel that has been published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extracts' looks like a noun, quoted passages, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To root out is to dig up or remove completely, the same as extracting.

clue.text: Fired after cutting of pay, fibre remaining though damaged

indicators.note: cutting into a word puts the cutter inside it

parts.note: to pay out is to spend
fired as in set alight

explanation.surface: A worker sacked after a pay cut, still hanging on though hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' suggests dismissal, but it means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: A split end is a hair that has frayed at its tip, a fibre still attached though damaged.

clue.text: Jolly chap, it's understood?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Jolly ..., the pirate flag, read as if it were a cheerful man
second meaning: radio-speak for message received

explanation.surface: Someone checks they have understood that a fellow is a cheerful sort.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jolly Roger is the skull-and-crossbones flag; here it is read as a jolly man called Roger, which was also Rufus's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio operators say this word to confirm a message has been received, and it completes the pirate flag's name.

clue.text: A jammed cylinder?

parts.note: surface reading: a stuck piston or engine part
setter's reading: a rolled sponge cake with a spiral of jam inside

explanation.surface: A mechanic's complaint about a seized cylinder in an engine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jammed' means stuck in the workshop but filled with jam at the tea table; this is one of Rufus's best-known clues.
explanation.definitionFit: The cake is a thin sponge spread with jam and rolled into a log, so it is literally a cylinder containing jam.

clue.text: Foremost of compilers with clue to set sadly leaves

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone badly wrong, so these letters are put out of order
the foremost part of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of compilers
taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A compiler mourns, having to leave behind the clue they were setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb about departing, but it is a noun: salad leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Cos lettuce is a long-leaved salad variety, so the phrase names a bunch of edible leaves.

clue.text: Listen up, 23 was perfect, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so each word gives only its final letter

parts.note: last letter of up
23 down is RUFUS; its last letter
last letter of was
last letter of perfect

explanation.surface: Pay attention: the setter of 23 down was simply perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listen up' reads as one phrase, but only 'Listen' is the definition; 'up' contributes its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Psst is the hushed sound used to catch someone's attention, an urgent call to listen.

clue.text: German outfit older, sheen tarnished

indicators.note: something tarnished is spoiled, so the letters lose their original order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A German garment ageing and losing its shine.
explanation.definitionFit: Lederhosen are the leather shorts with braces traditionally worn in Bavaria, a typical German outfit.

clue.text: Bar of soap?

parts.note: surface reading: a cake of soap for washing
setter's reading: the pub in a TV soap opera

explanation.surface: A simple bathroom item: a bar of soap.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar means a pub and soap means a TV serial; the pub is the one in Coronation Street, Britain's longest-running TV soap opera, set in a Manchester street.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rovers Return Inn is the fictional pub at the heart of Coronation Street, so it is literally the bar of a soap.

clue.text: Determined effort by solver?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: ... Morse, the TV detective and crossword fan

explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse's first name is Endeavour; he solves crimes and cryptic crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means a strenuous attempt, and it is also the first name of fiction's best-known crossword-solving detective.

clue.text: Set originally by other setters, they don't really work!

parts.note: to set something down is to place it

indicators.note: originally refers to how each word starts, its opening letter

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A puzzle first set by other compilers just doesn't work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' in a crossword tribute looks like the setter's job, but it is just the verb put.
explanation.definitionFit: Placebos are dummy pills with no active ingredient, so medically they do not really work.

clue.text: Out of sight, out of mind

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hidden beyond a curve in the road

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'out of sight, out of mind' is broken into two meanings of one idiom; another famous Rufus clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something past a curve cannot be seen, and the same idiom is informal British slang for insane.

clue.text: Sorcery of a wizard in the end so peerless, the ladies spotted?

indicators.note: sorcery transforms things, so the following letters are magically rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in the end points to the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of wizard
taken as written, ten letters

explanation.surface: Admiring a wizard's peerless magic, and noticing some women in the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' seems to mean seen, but it describes the big cats' spotted coats.
explanation.definitionFit: Leopardesses are female leopards, which are spotted animals, so they are spotted ladies.

clue.text: Chopstick?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, from the front half Chop: to split apart
second meaning, from the back half stick: to cling to

explanation.walkthrough: Chopstick reads as one eating utensil; split it, and the answer is a verb with two opposite meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleave is a contronym: it means both split with a blade and adhere closely to something.

clue.text: Monday's cryptic powerhouse …

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling or obscured, so the letters come disguised in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The driving force behind the Monday cryptic puzzle, continued into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Rufus set the Guardian's Monday cryptic for decades, so the surface describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynamo is a generator of power, and figuratively a tirelessly energetic person, a powerhouse.

clue.text: Stick veteran English player on the radio?

indicators.note: on the radio we only hear words, so the spelling may differ from the sound

parts.note: Michael Caine, the long-serving English film actor

explanation.surface: Sticking with an old English footballer or cricketer heard on a radio broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a sportsman, but it means an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A cane is a walking stick or a rod, so it is a kind of stick.

clue.text: Cheese ending in lake, fish rolling around it

indicators.note: around it says the fish surrounds the letter just taken

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so just that is taken

parts.note: last letter of lake
rolling country is hilly

explanation.surface: A cheese ending up in a lake, with a fish rolling about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling' looks like a description of the fish's motion; it is a separate piece, as in rolling hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Caerphilly is a crumbly white Welsh cheese named after the town where it originated.

clue.text: … author of 10, 14, 17 24 and 19 with setter's surface raised high — and so say all of __ !

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: a setter is a dog, and its coat is its outer surface
the song ends 'and so say all of us'

explanation.surface: A toast to the author of famous clues, raised high with a chorus of 'For he's a jolly good fellow'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' points at a crossword compiler, but it is the dog breed. The blank completes the song's last line.
explanation.definitionFit: Rufus was the pseudonym of Roger Squires, who wrote the clues for those entries.

clue.text: See 17
Casino visitor on vacation — counting winnings?

parts.note: one who bets
someone on holiday is off work

explanation.surface: A gambler on holiday sits tallying up what he has won.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone counting winnings is wealthier than before, which is the sense of the adjective phrase.

clue.text: First of all, so caring as protecting Anna — it goes with a flow

indicators.note: first of all asks for the first letter of every word that follows

parts.note: initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A caring person protecting someone called Anna, going along with things.
explanation.walkthrough: Scapa Flow is the great natural harbour in Orkney, so this word goes with Flow.
explanation.definitionFit: The word pairs with Flow to name the Orkney anchorage, so it literally goes with a flow.

clue.text: Fine Shropshire lad for starters, one taking final bow?

indicators.note: starters are the opening letters of each of the preceding words

parts.note: first letters of the two words
one who ends, as a performer closing the show

explanation.surface: A fine young man from Shropshire takes his last bow on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A Shropshire Lad is Housman's poem cycle; Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine can mean thin or delicate, as in a fine thread, which matches slender.

clue.text: Oarsmen at sea somewhere along the Mediterranean coast

indicators.note: at sea means confused and disoriented, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rowers out on the water off the Mediterranean shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanremo is a resort town on the Italian Riviera, so it lies on the Mediterranean coast.
